segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or do you not know, brothers and sisters (for I am speaking to people who know the law), that the law rules over a person for as long as that person lives?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law concerning her husband.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, while her husband lives she will be called an adulteress if she becomes another man’s; but if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is not an adulteress when she becomes another man’s.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So, my brothers and sisters, you too were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might become another’s, his who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit for God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions that came through the law were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now we have been released from the law, having died to what held us fast, so that we serve as slaves in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! Yet I would not have known sin except through the law. For I would not have known coveting if the law had not said,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You shall not covet.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of coveting. For apart from law sin is dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I was once alive apart from law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and I died, and the very commandment that was meant for life was found, in my case, to lead to death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Did what is good, then, become death for me? Certainly not! Rather, it was sin, so that it might be shown to be sin, producing death in me through what is good, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am made of flesh, sold under sin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I do not understand what I carry out. For I do not practice what I want; instead, what I hate is what I do.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as it is, it is no longer I who carry it out, but sin that lives in me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh. For the wanting lies close at hand for me, but carrying out the good does not.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I do not do the good that I want; instead, the evil that I do not want is what I practice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who carry it out, but sin that lives in me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I find this law: when I want to do good, evil lies close at hand for me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I delight in the law of God in my inner self,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but I see a different law in my members, waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What a wretched person I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself with my mind serve the law of God as a slave, but with my flesh the law of sin.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole Roman community. 'Brothers' alone would suggest to a modern reader that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep 'brothers' with a footnote.

'Flesh' in Paul often means more than the physical body: it is human existence in its weakness and its orientation away from God. 'When we were in the flesh' describes a former condition of life, not simply being alive in a body. Some translations paraphrase it as 'sinful nature', but the traditional word is kept here because Paul's contrast with 'Spirit' depends on it.

The verb is the ordinary one for doing a slave's service and picks up the slavery language of the previous chapter (6:16–22). 'Serve' alone loses that connection. Most translations have 'serve'; a few have 'are slaves' or similar.

notes.phrase: in the newness of the Spirit
notes.traditional: in newness of spirit / in the new way of the Spirit
notes.note: Greek manuscripts did not distinguish capital letters, so the word may be God's Spirit or the human spirit. Most interpreters take it as the Holy Spirit, anticipating chapter 8, and that reading is followed here. 'The letter' means the law as a written code.

notes.phrase: I would not have known sin
notes.note: Who the 'I' of verses 7–25 is has been debated since antiquity. It may be Paul's own experience, a representative voice for Adam, for Israel under the law, or for humanity generally. It is also disputed whether verses 14–25, in the present tense, describe life before or after coming to Christ. The translation leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

Paul quotes the opening of the tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 5:21) without its list of objects. The Greek noun here and in verse 8 comes from the same root as the verb in the commandment, so 'coveting' and 'covet' keep the link visible. The word covers wrongful desire of any kind, not only sexual desire, which 'lust' now suggests.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: 'righteous' and 'just', 'righteousness' and 'justice', come from the same root. Older English versions have 'just' here. The sense is that the commandment is in the right and requires what is right.

The image is of the slave market: a person sold passes into the power of the buyer. Sin is pictured as the owner, continuing the slavery language of chapter 6. Some translations spell this out as 'sold as a slave to sin'.

Most interpreters take 'law' here in a looser sense, a rule or regular pattern, and many translations say 'principle'. Others hold that Paul still means the law of Moses: 'I find, as regards the law, that when I want to do good, evil lies close at hand.' 'Law' is kept so that the reader can see Paul using one word throughout verses 21–25.

notes.traditional: the body of this death / this body of death
notes.note: In the Greek, 'this' can attach either to 'body' or to 'death', giving 'the body of this death', as in older versions. The difference is small. Either way the phrase means the body as the place where sin and death hold sway.

Manuscripts differ here: some read 'Thanks be to God', others 'I thank God', the reading behind the King James Version. Still others have 'the grace of God', which turns the phrase into an answer to the question in verse 24. Most modern editions prefer 'Thanks be to God', and the sense is little affected.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translators split between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'friends'.
Paul's theological use is rendered variously ('flesh', 'sinful nature', 'human nature'), and readers need to see one word across Romans, Galatians and elsewhere.
A favourite Pauline verb rendered very differently by context (release, nullify, abolish, bring to nothing); a governed set of renderings per sense would keep the letters consistent.
Whether to render 'serve' or 'be a slave' affects the δοῦλος word-group across the whole New Testament and should be decided once.
This fixed formula of strong denial recurs in Romans, 1 Corinthians and Galatians and should read identically each time ('By no means', 'God forbid', 'Certainly not').
